headline: High: Cursor’s default filesystem/MCP access can feed LangGraph workflows, creating dangerous prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor ingests workspace files, open buffers, clipboard, and MCP outputs by default, while LangGraph can route developer-defined tool outputs through graph nodes. That creates a direct path for attacker-controlled content from Cursor into LangGraph prompts or tools. Because the bridge is shared filesystem/clipboard/MCP and no provenance tracking is stated, injection risk is high.
conditions: IF Cursor content is copied into a LangGraph node prompt without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF a shared MCP server or workspace is used as the bridge, attacker-controlled text can reach LangGraph instructions.
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the tools.
Add a strict prompt wrapper that quotes all Cursor-derived text.
Use a provenance tag or allowlist before LangGraph consumes any Cursor output.
Run LangGraph on a separate workspace copy.
requires-engineering: add content-type validation at every Cursor→LangGraph boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents, and LangGraph can persist graph state in a checkpointer store. If the same workspace or state store is reused, sensitive code or notes can flow from Cursor into LangGraph persistence or model-provider calls. The pathway exists in default-style setups, but the blast radius is bounded to project data rather than guaranteed external exfiltration.
conditions: IF both agents share the same project directory or checkpointer-backed state, Cursor content can be retained by LangGraph.
IF LangGraph nodes forward stored state to model providers, sensitive snippets may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Clear or rotate the LangGraph checkpointer store before sensitive runs.
Exclude secrets and clipboard contents from Cursor sessions.
Restrict LangGraph state to minimal fields only.
requires-engineering: encrypt and scope the checkpointer per project.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files and execute shells; Cursor also modifies git state, while LangGraph can run developer-defined tools and persist shared state. In a shared directory, concurrent writes or git operations can race and corrupt work or history. Because Cursor explicitly supports local filesystem sharing and LangGraph supports multiple instances with persistent state, the conflict is substantial.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent commits or rewrites can conflict.
IF LangGraph nodes and Cursor both write the same files, last-writer-wins corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout or branch.
Serialize file writes with a lock file.
Disable Cursor Yolo mode during shared edits.
Pause LangGraph writes while Cursor is active.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around git and filesystem mutations.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate code, edits, and tool-driven suggestions, and LangGraph can treat upstream node outputs as inputs to later nodes or actions. If LangGraph consumes Cursor output without verification, mistakes or hallucinations can cascade into shell actions, file writes, or downstream agent steps. The pair therefore has a strong default pathway from unverified output to action.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses Cursor output as a node input without validation, errors can propagate.
IF a downstream LangGraph node executes shell or writes files based on that output, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before any action node.
Require schema validation on Cursor outputs.
Mark Cursor outputs as untrusted in LangGraph state.
Limit downstream nodes to read-only analysis.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks before execution nodes.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor handles clipboard contents and source code, while LangGraph persists graph state in a checkpointer store and may send state to model providers. If regulated or sensitive data is placed in Cursor and then stored or processed by LangGraph, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR status, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into Cursor and then persisted by LangGraph, retention policy mismatch can occur.
IF the checkpointer store is hosted in a different jurisdiction than the source data, residency issues can arise.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs.
Purge LangGraph checkpoints after each session.
Keep Cursor sessions free of secrets and clipboard PII.
Document the storage region for the checkpointer.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls across both systems.
